The install script downloads the build for your CPU, checks it against SHA256SUMS, and puts it at ~/.local/bin/concord. Nothing runs as root. Running concord opens your browser on the app. Set PREFIX to install somewhere other than ~/.local/bin; the script warns if that directory is not on your PATH. Running the script again updates in place, and so does the app itself (see Updates). To install by hand, download concord-linux-amd64-<version> or concord-linux-arm64-<version>, make it executable with chmod +x, and run it.

Download concord-desktop-linux-<version>, make it executable, and run it. It needs WebKitGTK 4.1 (the webkit2gtk-4.1 package on most distributions). The first time you run it from anywhere else, it installs itself for your user: the program goes to ~/.local/share/concord, and a launcher entry and icon are added so Concord shows up in your application menu. It then restarts from that location. A copy under /usr, /opt, /nix, /snap or /app is left where it is, since a package manager owns those paths. To remove the installed copy, run it with --uninstall. There is no sign-up. The first time Concord opens on a device, it asks for two things: Your name: what other people see, up to 32 characters. You can change it later. A passphrase, typed twice. It encrypts your identity and your messages on this device. A meter rates its strength, but nothing is enforced; a few unrelated words is a good passphrase. Select Create identity. Concord generates your identity, a cryptographic key pair, and shows your recovery phrase: 24 words that can rebuild that key on any device. Each time Concord starts, it asks for your passphrase and you select Unlock. On a phone you can turn on biometric unlock after the first unlock. What "an account" means in Concord: a key pair you hold rather than a record on a server, the passphrase that protects it on each device, the recovery phrase that can rebuild it, and the profile other people see.

Concord has no sign-up, no email address, no username registry and no server that knows you exist. Your account is a cryptographic key: an Ed25519 key pair generated on your device the first time you create an identity. Holding the private key is what makes you you. Nobody can suspend the account, rename it or reset it, and nobody can recover it for you if the key is lost. Everything else follows from that key. Your network address is derived from it, so a connection to you can only be completed by a device holding it. Every message you send is signed with it, so other members can check that i

Other people recognize your key by its fingerprint, also called a safety number: 32 letters and digits in groups of four, derived from your public key. It is the same on every device you link, because it comes from the account key. You can see your own at the bottom of Settings → Your profile, under "Your identity fingerprint". To check someone else's, open their profile card, reveal their safety number, and compare it with them over a channel you trust, such as in person or on a call. If they match, select Verify identity. Verification is a note you keep for yourself on your own devices; nobo

The passphrase protects your identity on one device. Concord stretches it with Argon2id (64 MiB of memory per guess) into a key that encrypts your identity file, so someone who copies the file still has to guess the passphrase, and each guess is expensive. Your local message database is encrypted under a key derived from your identity, so it is unreadable without unlocking too. Message text and attachments are sealed. Some details are stored unencrypted: who sent each message and when, display names, guild and channel names, reactions, profile pictures, read positions and settings. Someone wit

The recovery phrase is your account key written as 24 words from the standard BIP-39 word list. It is shown once when the identity is created, and you can reveal it again at any time in Settings → Account → Recovery phrase. Anyone who has these words can become you, on any device, without your passphrase. Keep them offline and never share them. The phrase brings back the key, and only the key. A device restored from it is you, to everyone who has verified you, but it starts with no profile, no guilds and no history. Backups and recovery explains how to get those back.

You can use the same account on a computer and a phone at once. Each device keeps its own device key alongside the shared account key, and the account key signs a certificate saying the device belongs to you. Other members see one person, not two. Multiple devices covers linking, what is shared, and removing a device.
How to use one account on several devices: linking a new device with a QR code, what it receives and what stays separate afterwards, and how to remove a device you no longer use or no longer have.

A linked device is not a copy of another one. Each device has its own device key, generated on it and never sent anywhere. When you link, your existing device signs a certificate saying the new device key belongs to your account, and hands over the account key. The new device then joins each of your guilds as its own member, under your account. Other people see one person with one fingerprint, whichever device you use. Linking needs both devices online at the same time and able to reach each other. On the same network that is immediate; across the internet it goes through a rendezvous and can

On the device that already has your account, open Settings → Link a device. It shows a QR code and a Copy code instead button. On the new device, at the first-run screen, choose Link to an existing account. Select Scan QR code and point the camera at the code, or paste the copied code into the box. Scan QR code appears on touch-screen devices with a camera, such as a phone; on a computer, paste the code. Choose a passphrase for the new device and type it twice. It protects your identity on that device only and does not have to match the passphrase on your other devices. Select Link this device

At the moment of linking, your existing device sends: the account key and the certificate for the new device; your profile; your rendezvous address; the list of people you have verified; an invitation to every guild and direct-message conversation on the existing device, except direct messages you have hidden. The new device joins each of those through the guild's normal admission path, then catches up on history from the members who are online, your other devices included. Some things are deliberately local: Settings and appearance: theme, colors, notification choices, microphone and camera, push-to-talk key. In the single-file build these belong to the browser profile you open it in. Saved messages (bookmarks) never leave the device they were saved on. A backup carries them. Message history settings: a guild's retention rule is applied by each device to its own copy. The passphrase, and on Android the biometric unlock.

Settings → Connection → Stats & diagnostics opens the diagnostics panel; Ctrl+Shift+, opens it directly. Its Your devices section lists every device signed in to the account: its name, the version it runs, whether it is online or when it was last seen, and how it is connected. The device you are using is marked this one.

In Your devices, select Unlink next to the device and confirm. Unlinking takes effect in two parts: Immediately, the device is removed from all your guilds and stops receiving anything new. Whoever holds it cannot undo that. The next time it comes online with Concord running, the device erases its own copy of your identity, guilds and messages, and shows a notice that it was unlinked. A device that stays off keeps what it had already downloaded, and nothing can reach it to delete it. If a device was lost or stolen, treat everything on it as already read. What can be recovered if you lose a device or forget your passphrase, and how: the recovery phrase for your identity, linked devices and backup files for your history, and Markdown export for a readable copy.

Concord keeps no copy of anything on a server. Two separate things live on your devices, and each has its own way back: WhatRecovered byYour identity (the account key)The 24-word recovery phrase, or another linked deviceYour guilds, conversations and historyAnother linked device, a backup file, or rejoining and syncing from other members The two are recovered separately on purpose. The recovery phrase holds no messages, and a backup file holds no identity. Settings → Account puts both under "Your safety net": Backup & restore and Recovery phrase. The most complete safety net is a second linked

Your recovery phrase is your account key written as 24 words. It is shown when the identity is created and can be revealed again in Settings → Account → Recovery phrase. Write it down on paper or in a password manager. To use it on a new or reset device, choose Restore from a recovery phrase on the first-run screen, enter the 24 words, choose a new passphrase for the device, and select Restore account. What comes back is the key: you are the same person, with the same fingerprint, to everyone who has verified you. What does not come back is everything else. The restored device starts with no n
A backup file is a sealed copy of the history on one device. Make one in Settings → Account → Backup & restore.

Under Make a backup, choose a passphrase for the file (at least 8 characters) and repeat it. It can be different from your app passphrase. Optionally tick Include images and files. Select Download backup. The file is saved as concord-backup-<date>.archive. The backup contains every guild and direct-message conversation on the device, your Notes, and your saved messages. It is compressed, then encrypted under the file passphrase with the same construction that protects your identity on disk (Argon2id and XSalsa20-Poly1305). There is no way to recover a lost file passphrase. Include images and f

Make sure the device is signed in and has rejoined the guilds you want history for. In Settings → Account → Backup & restore, under Restore a backup, enter the archive's passphrase. Select Choose a backup file… and pick the .archive file. Restoring only adds. Nothing already on the device is overwritten or removed, so restoring an old backup cannot lose newer messages, and restoring the same file twice does nothing the second time. History is restored only into guilds and conversations this device is a member of; the rest is counted as skipped. Your Notes and saved messages come back regardles

Export writes a readable transcript, not a restorable backup. It is plain text, unencrypted, and one-way: use it to keep, print or share a conversation. One channel: open the More menu in the channel header and choose Export history. It saves <channel>-history.md. A whole guild: Guild settings → Data → Export history shows the file name, size and message count, then saves every channel as one <guild>-history.md file, including any history the guild imported from elsewhere. Exports are read from the full local history, not just what is on screen. Pictures, files and voice messages are named in

Everything comes back.Use my recovery phraseErases this device's data, then restores your identity under a new passphrase. If the lost device was linked to another of yours, unlink it from the remaining one (see Remove a device). That removes it from your guilds straight away. It erases its own copy only if it comes back online running Concord, so treat whatever was on it as exposed. If it was your only device, restore your identity from the recovery phrase on a new one, rejoin your guilds, and restore your latest backup file. Without the recovery phrase and without another linked device, the identity cannot be recovered by anyone.

How to create a guild, invite people and join one, organize channels and categories, and use messages, threads, polls and events. It also covers leaving a guild, handing it over, and importing an older community's history. A guild is a shared, end-to-end-encrypted space with its own channels and members. It is not hosted anywhere: every member's device holds a copy, and the guild keeps running as long as members keep using it. + → Poll opens the poll editor: a Question (up to 300 characters), 2 to 10 Options (up to 100 characters each), Allow selecting multiple options, Closes (Never, 1 hour, 24 hours or 3 days), and Quiz mode, where one option is the correct answer. Votes travel as reactions, signed by the voter like any message, so polls are not anonymous.

In a text channel, Start thread on a message (or + → Start a thread) opens a side conversation with its own title (up to 200 bytes) and unread count. A thread started from a message quotes it and links back to it. Threads do not get their own row in the channel list; their unread counts add to the parent channel's row. Forum posts are threads too; see Forum boards.

Disappearing messages… in a channel's or conversation's menu sets a timer of 5 minutes, 1 hour, 8 hours, 1 day or 1 week (or Off). It is your choice for this conversation: messages you send afterwards carry the expiry and are erased on every device when it passes.

Guild settings → Events & calendar (or the calendar button in the chat header) holds the guild's shared calendar. Any member can create an event with a title, details, start time, duration, location (a place or one of the guild's channels) and a repeat rule: Never, Every day, Every week, Every other week or Every month. Members answer Going, Maybe or No, and the event's menu offers Add to calendar (.ics). The author can edit or delete an event, and so can anyone with Manage messages.

Choose Leave guild from the guild's right-click menu, the chat header menu, or Guild settings → Danger zone. Your copy of the guild's messages is deleted from this device. Everyone else keeps theirs, and the guild keeps running. The guild will not come back on its own, including through your linked devices. Rejoining takes a new invite. To keep the text, use Guild settings → Export history first. It writes every channel to one unencrypted Markdown file. There is no way to delete a guild for everyone.

The button reads Leave and delete my copy. Ownership cannot be appointed after you leave, so before leaving, use Guild settings → Ownership & heir: Transfer ownership… hands the guild to another member immediately. It is one-way; only the new owner can hand it back. Name an heir… gives a member a standing, revocable right to Take ownership at any time. Use Revoke to withdraw it. Any change of owner clears the heir.

How a guild decides who may do what: the owner, named roles, the seven permissions a role can grant, and the rank rules that stop anyone granting themselves more power than they have.

The owner holds every permission and outranks every role. A guild has exactly one owner at a time; ownership moves only by transfer or by an heir claiming it (see Leaving a guild). Everyone else gets their powers from roles. A role is a name, a color and a set of permissions. A member can hold several roles, and their permissions add up. A member with no role can read and post, react, start threads and forum posts, create events and use the guild's emoji and GIFs. Everything in the table below needs a role that grants it. Guild settings → Members lists everyone, sortable by Name, Roles, Standing and Fingerprint. The owner and members with Manage roles can add and remove roles there, for one member or a selection. A member's profile card and right-click menu offer Make admin (or Remove admin) to the owner and to anyone who holds every permission. It assigns a role named Admin that grants all seven permissions, creating it first if the guild has none. Roles also work as mention groups: @rolename in a message notifies everyone who holds the role.

A member's rank is the highest position among their roles. A member with no roles ranks below everyone; the owner ranks above everyone. For anyone but the owner: You can only create or edit a role below your own rank, and only with permissions you already hold. You can only delete or assign roles below your own rank. Nobody but the owner can give the owner a role. Nobody can ban, kick or mute the owner. A ban removes all of the member's roles. Together these mean a member with Manage roles cannot raise themselves: any role they make is capped at their own permissions and must rank below them.

There is no server to refuse an action, so each rule is checked on every member's device. Removing a member from the encrypted group is a real cryptographic step: once kicked or banned they cannot read new messages. Mutes, slow mode, announcement-only posting and closed forum posts work differently: each member's app drops the messages that break them. A modified client can still send such a message, but no honest member's app will show it.
A forum channel is a board of posts, each with its own title and thread of replies. This page covers writing posts, tags, answered and closed posts, and sorting, filtering and laying out a board.
A member with Manage channels creates one like any channel: + beside Channels → New channel → Forum. The Study group guild template includes a #questions forum. See Guilds and channels.

How to talk, turn on a camera and share your screen in voice channels, direct-message calls and meetings, how to set up your microphone and push-to-talk, and how calls connect: directly between participants, or through a relay that hides your IP address.

Every call is a mesh: each participant's app opens a direct, encrypted WebRTC connection to every other participant. Audio and video are encrypted end to end with DTLS-SRTP and never pass through any Concord server, because there is none. The app only uses your peers and your rendezvous to arrange the connection. A mesh means you send one copy of your audio and video to each person in the call. Concord sets no limit on how many people can join, but the upload your connection needs grows with every participant, so calls work best in small rooms. h: How moderation works without a server
t: There is no company and no central moderation team in Concord. A guild is moderated by its own owner and the members they give permissions to. Every moderation decision (a kick, a ban, a role change) is a signed entry in the guild's governance log. Every member's app replays that log and checks each signature and permission itself, so a decision that the person making it was not allowed to make is ignored everywhere. What Concord encrypts, who can see what, what a rendezvous node learns, and what stays unprotected, in plain language. The formal policy is PRIVACY.md; the engineering detail is DESIGN.md, especially §13 Threat model.

There is no account database and no company server. Your identity is a keypair made on your device. Your messages go directly between the people in the conversation, end-to-end encrypted. No one else can read them, including the operator of any rendezvous node you use. Your history is stored on your own devices, with message bodies encrypted under your passphrase. Who you talk to, and when, is not hidden. Peers you connect to directly see your IP address.

Every guild is one encrypted group, using MLS (Messaging Layer Security, RFC 9420). Every direct message, including group DMs and your own Notes, is its own MLS group too. Only the current members hold the keys. Messages, edits, deletions, reactions, pins and the history batches a member sends you when you catch up after being offline are all encrypted to the group. Forward secrecy. Old keys are deleted as the group moves on, so a key stolen today cannot decrypt traffic recorded last month. Removing someone re-keys the group. It is never a member of any group and holds no message keys, so it cannot read messages, attachments, history or calls. How to decide whether your group needs a rendezvous node, and how to run one locally, with Docker, on a VPS or on fly.io. Two Concord peers can only talk if at least one of them can accept an incoming connection. On the same Wi-Fi that is free. Across the internet, home routers usually refuse, and something has to introduce the two sides. That something is a rendezvous: a small always-on node that helps peers find each other and forwards their traffic when neither can be dialled directly. It is not a server in the sense Concord is arguing against — it holds no accounts, stores no history, and

If you and your friends are on a Tailscale tailnet — or any WireGuard mesh — you need no rendezvous at all. Every machine gets a stable address that every other machine can dial directly, which is precisely the thing home routers refuse to provide. Start Concord normally on each machine; there is nothing to configure. Concord listens on every network interface, the tailnet one included, and invite codes carry this machine's network addresses, so a code handed to someone on the same tailnet carries an address they can dial. This is the best option for a private group: no public infrastructure,

h: What if I lose my device?
t: If the account is linked on another device, link the new one from it and your guilds and history come with it. The phrase restores your identity only: the new device starts with no guilds and no history, so ask someone in each guild for a fresh invite, then restore a backup file (Settings → Account → Backup & restore) if you made one. Without the phrase and without another linked device, the identity cannot be recovered; there is no one to ask.

h: Do messages arrive while I am offline?
t: If a rendezvous is set, every message, in a guild or a direct message, is also deposited, encrypted, in the rendezvous mailbox of each member device that is offline, and collected when that device comes back. The mailbox keeps them in memory for up to 14 days. Anything it does not hold is synced from whichever members are online when you reconnect.

t: Concord is built for friend groups and communities. Calls are a full mesh, where every participant sends to every other, which suits a handful of people per call.

How Concord's code is layered, from the Svelte UI down through the Go core to the network, and how the same core is packaged as a desktop window, a browser-served binary, a phone app and a headless client. Concord architecture Three shells host the Svelte UI, which talks HTTP and SSE to internal/httpapi; that calls internal/bridge, which wraps the internal/app Service; the Service sits on the domain, store, crypto and network layers, which reach the vendored MLS library, other peers and the rendezvous. The core lives under internal/. Each layer depends only on the ones below it. PackageRoleinternal/identityEd25519 account and device keys, device certificates, the Argon2id keystore, BIP39 recovery wordsinternal/crypto/mlsThe group-encryption engine: a small Engine interface over the vendored MLS library in third_party/mls-gointernal/domainThe pure data model (guilds, channels, messages) and topic-name derivation. No I/Ointernal/storeThe local SQLite database, with message bodies sealed at restinternal/netThe libp2p host: mDNS and DHT discovery, circuit relay, gossipsub, and the /concord/* str

internal/net wraps a single libp2p host per process. Peers find each other three ways: mDNS on the local network (service tag concord._mdns._v1), a Kademlia DHT under the key concord/dht/v1, and addresses carried inside invite codes. A peer behind a NAT is reached through a circuit relay until hole punching gives a direct connection; a peer that learns it is publicly reachable also relays for members of its own guilds. §4 and §5 of DESIGN.md cover why. Live traffic travels on gossipsub topics; everything that is point-to-point travels on a dedicated stream protocol. Protocol and data model lis

Each guild, DM, group DM and meeting is one MLS group (RFC 9420). internal/crypto/mls hides the library behind an Engine interface (CreateGroup, Invite, AddMembers, Join, ApplyCommit, Encrypt, Decrypt, and so on), so the rest of the core never touches MLS types. The library is vendored under third_party/mls-go and wired in with a replace in go.mod; its local changes are recorded in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md.

internal/store is SQLite through modernc.org/sqlite, a pure-Go driver, so no build needs a C toolchain for it. Message bodies are sealed with NaCl secretbox under a key derived from the unlocked identity; structural metadata is stored in the clear so it can be queried and ordered. The database is concord.db in the data directory, next to keystore.json. CONCORD_HOME overrides the data directory, which is how make peers runs several isolated peers on one machine.

internal/app is where features live. Service starts the libp2p host, subscribes to each guild's topics, runs the background loops (history reconcile, stranded-guild healing, mailbox drains), and exposes plain Go methods for everything the UI can do. Its files are named after features: guild.go, dm.go, sync.go, governance.go, voice.go, mailbox.go, invite.go, link.go, forum.go, and so on.

The UI never calls the Service directly. internal/bridge wraps the Service and translates domain types into JSON-friendly view structs. The libp2p protocols Concord speaks, what travels on each, how peers catch up on history, and how a peer stores what it has seen. DESIGN.md has the reasoning; this page is the map.

Peers exchange data in two ways. Gossipsub topics carry live group traffic: every member of a guild subscribes to the guild's topics and publishes MLS ciphertext to them. A message reaches everyone online at that moment, and nobody else. Stream protocols carry anything point-to-point: a join handshake, a history catch-up, an attachment download, a call setup. Each is a libp2p stream protocol under /concord/. A peer that missed gossip recovers it through the sync stream, or from the mailbox on the rendezvous if no member was online to ask.

Topic names are derived in internal/domain/model.go. Each is concord/c/ followed by the first 16 bytes, in hex, of a SHA-256 over the MLS group ID and a suffix, so a topic name reveals neither the guild nor its group ID to the pubsub network, while every member derives the same value. A chat message is a JSON-encoded domain.Message (internal/domain/model.go): ID, channel ID, sender account key, display name, Kind, ReplyTo, content, send time, and flags for edited, deleted and pinned. The author signs it (Sig) before it is MLS-encrypted and published to the channel topic. A sealed copy is also deposited in the mailbox of each member who is offline. Message actions are messages too. A Kind of edit, delete, reaction or pin acts on the message named in ReplyTo, and system marks a notice. An edit carries RowSig, the author's signature over the row as it will read after the edit.

The meta topic carries a guildMeta envelope (internal/app/guild.go) whose type names the change: channel_added, channel_updated, channel_renamed, channel_removed, category_added, category_renamed, category_removed, emoji_added, emoji_removed, guild_renamed, profile, nickname, event_upserted, story, chronicle, gov_op, and others. receiveGuildMeta is the full list.

The checks a change has to pass, exactly as CI runs them, and the slower suites and harnesses for what the gate does not cover: the network integration tests, local multi-peer runs, and the browser end-to-end scripts. CI is defined in .github/workflows/ci.yml. It runs on every push to main, on every pull request, nightly, and on manual dispatch. It has three jobs: frontend and backend run every time, and integration runs only on the nightly schedule or a manual dispatch.

Lint runs ESLint over frontend/src/**/*.{js,mjs,svelte}. The rule that matters is no-undef: a reference to something that does not exist compiles cleanly and fails only at runtime, in the user's window. Build is the production Vite build. It has to succeed, because every shipped artifact embeds or copies its output. Test runs each frontend/src/lib/*.test.mjs file with plain Node. There is no test framework; each file is a script that exits non-zero when a case fails. The files are listed one by one in the test script in frontend/package.json, so a new test file runs only once it is added there

The Go binary embeds frontend/dist, which is not tracked, so this job builds the frontend before anything else: gofmt fails the job if any Go file outside third_party/ is not formatted. third_party/ is vendored and keeps upstream's formatting; never reformat it. make fmt runs gofmt -w on the root .go files, internal/ and cmd/. It does not touch mobile/ or scripts/, which CI still checks, so run gofmt -w on those directly if you change them. The full Go suite, including every testing.Short()-guarded test, under the race detector. -p 1 runs one package at a time so packages do not compete for the CPU. Concord is a peer-to-peer, end-to-end-encrypted chat app: a Go core (identity, MLS, libp2p, storage) with a Svelte UI that the same core serves either into a browser or into a native desktop window. Before changing anything substantial, read docs/DESIGN.md. It is long on purpose. It explains why the design is the way it is, and most of the questions a newcomer has ("why is there a server at all?", "why can't two people commit at once?") are answered there rather than in the code. h: Signing, and why the host stops mattering
t: Release trust is a signature, not a source. SHA256SUMS lists every asset's hash, so signing that one file covers all of them. Releases are signed with an offline Ed25519 key whose public half is compiled into every binary (internal/bridge/release-pubkey.txt); a client verifies the signature over SHA256SUMS first, then checks the download against the now-trusted hash, never the other way round. Because a signature is what is trusted, where the bytes came from stops mattering, which is what makes peer-to-peer updates safe: a peer already running the newer build can hand you the same bytes, as a

Binaries are published to this repository's own Releases, which is also what the in-app update check polls (internal/bridge/update.go). That poll is unauthenticated, so no token is ever embedded in a shipped binary, and the workflow signs in with the run's built-in GITHUB_TOKEN under permissions: contents: write. There is no personal access token to create, scope or rotate, and a fork can cut its own releases with no secrets configured.

Unsigned executables lose SmartScreen reputation on every new build. After each release, submit concord-desktop-windows-vX.Y.Z.exe to https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/filesubmission as an incorrectly detected file, which whitelists that build's hash in Defender. It has to be redone every release, because every release is a new hash. The durable fix is code signing, deferred on cost. WINDOWS.md has the user-facing bypass and the web-binary fallback.

The rendezvous is deployed separately and rarely (fly deploy -c fly.rendezvous.toml), and its seed never changes.

Concord is a peer-to-peer group chat, voice and video application: a Go core with a Svelte front end, shipped as one binary. There is no company, no account database, and no server that stores your messages. Every guild ("server") is a cryptographic group, every message is end-to-end encrypted, and the one piece of infrastructure it can use is untrusted by construction. This document is the design paper. It explains what peer-to-peer means for each job a server normally does, defines every term the first time it appears, and describes each mechanism precisely enough that you could argue with i

Centralized chat platforms have a structural property that no privacy policy can fix: the operator sits between every message you send and every friend who reads it. The operator authenticates you, stores your history, relays your voice, and, with the best intentions in the world, can read, mine, moderate, lose, leak, or be compelled to hand over all of it. Transport encryption (TLS) does not change this: the server terminates TLS, so the plaintext exists on the operator's machines by design. Availability, privacy, history and membership are promises the operator makes to you, not guarantees y

Concord ships stories, a soundboard, a meme editor, polls, events, calendars, more than twenty themes and a game collection for your profile. It is not a minimal application. It is a self-contained one: one binary, no external services, no runtime fetches by default, no account database. Features are built to hold that line rather than trimmed to avoid testing it. The soundboard synthesizes its sounds from oscillators instead of shipping audio files. Emoji and typefaces are compiled in rather than requested from a CDN. Story backgrounds are drawn presets, not stock images pulled down on demand

No account database. Your identity is a keypair on your device. There is nothing to sign up for, no email, no phone number, no username table, and nothing to breach. No message store. History lives on the devices of the people in the conversation and nowhere else. No trusted server. There is one optional piece of infrastructure (§6). It is cryptographically incapable of reading what it carries, and the system is designed to survive its loss. No runtime fetches. No fonts, no emoji images, no analytics, no crash reporting, no update ping to anything except the release repository you can see. A r

Concord targets friend groups and communities, not million-user servers. Text scales fine; a full mesh of live audio connections does not scale to stadiums, and does not need to. That single trade is what buys everything else, and it is stated up front rather than discovered later.

h: Why the difficulty is worth it
t: Because solving these problems among the participants means nobody else has to be trusted. Privacy stops being a policy the operator promises and becomes a property of the mathematics. Client–server is mailing every letter through one post office that photocopies each page "for safety". Peer-to-peer is handing your friend a sealed, tamper-evident envelope that only they can open, with no post office in the picture.

h: 3. Identity: a keypair is an account

t: On first run Concord generates 32 random bytes, a seed, and derives an Ed25519 keypair from it. Ed25519 is a digital-signature scheme: the private key can sign a message, and anyone holding the public key can verify that signature and cannot forge one. That keypair is the account. There is no row in a database that says the account exists; the account exists because you hold the key. Nobody can suspend it, rename it, or issue a second one. Nobody can help you if you lose it either, which is why the seed is also expressible as a 24-word BIP39 recovery phrase.

h: Your address is derived from your identity
t: Concord's networking is built on libp2p, a toolkit that gives every node a PeerID. For Ed25519 keys the public key is short enough that libp2p embeds it in the PeerID verbatim rather than hashing it, so a PeerID is a public key in disguise. This single fact removes an entire category of infrastructure. When you dial a peer, the transport handshake (Noise, the same construction WireGuard uses) proves the far end holds the private key for the PeerID you dialled. If it does not, the handshake fails. There is no certificate, no certificate authority, and nothing to revoke: the address is the ident

A PeerID is 52 characters of base58, fine for a machine and useless for reading aloud. So Concord also derives a fingerprint: The app calls this a safety number, which is the term the field has settled on for a fingerprint two people read to each other. Its purpose is narrow, and the narrowness matters: What it defends against. The one attack the mathematics cannot see is a substitution at first contact: an attacker who hands you their key while claiming to be your friend. Every subsequent guarantee then holds perfectly, for the wrong person. Comparing fingerprints over a channel the attacker

An account is the seed and the keypair derived from it: stable across every machine you use, and the thing fingerprints are computed from. A device is one installation. Each installation generates its own separate 32-byte device seed, which never leaves it. Linking a second device does not copy an identity so much as certify one: The certificate is signed by the account key over a length-prefixed, domain-separated encoding of its fields, so it cannot be replayed into another context. A linked device gets its own network address (its PeerID comes from its device key, so two devices of one accou

The seed is the only true secret, so it gets the strongest treatment on disk. It is sealed with NaCl secretbox (XSalsa20-Poly1305) under a key stretched from your passphrase with Argon2id: 64 MiB of memory, 3 passes, 4 lanes, a fresh 16-byte salt per save. Argon2id is memory-hard, so guessing your passphrase costs an attacker 64 MiB of RAM per guess, which is what makes offline brute-force expensive rather than free. The parameters are recorded in the file so they can be raised later without breaking existing keystores. The plaintext seed never touches disk. A wrong passphrase is indistinguish

h: 4. Discovery: what a distributed hash table is, and how Concord finds people
t: Alice wants to send Bob a message. Before anything else can happen she must learn a current address for him. This section is about that and nothing else.

A hash table maps keys to values. You hash the key to an index, and the value lives there. One machine holds the whole table; lookups are one step. A distributed hash table (DHT) spreads that same table across many machines with no coordinator. The design problem is a single question: given a key, which machine holds it? It has to be answered without asking anyone, because asking requires a directory, which is what we are building. Kademlia, the DHT design libp2p uses, answers it like this: Give every node an identifier from the same space as the keys. Node IDs and keys are both fixed-length b

XOR distance looks strange until you notice what it measures: the length of the shared prefix. XOR is symmetric (d(A,B) = d(B,A)), so if A is a useful contact for B, B is a useful contact for A, and every lookup that passes through a node teaches it something it can reuse. It is also unidirectional: for any key and any distance there is one identifier at that distance and no other, so lookups from different starting points converge on the same neighbourhood rather than wandering. And because distance is dominated by prefix length, the identifier space behaves like a binary tree with the keys a

h: 4.3 Why the routing takes O(log n) hops
t: Each node keeps its contacts in buckets by shared-prefix length: bucket i holds up to k peers whose IDs share the first i bits with its own and differ at the next. In Concord's DHT k = 20. So a node knows a great many peers "near" itself and only a handful in each successively more distant half of the space, a routing table of about log₂(n) buckets rather than n entries. A lookup for key K asks the closest contacts it knows (α = 10 in parallel) a single question: who do you know that is closer to K than you are? Each answer comes from a node with a longer shared prefix with K than the last, so

Nobody hands out DHT keys. They are computed, which is what makes independent nodes agree without talking: The key is a hash of the thing being looked up. Concord's namespace is the literal string concord/dht/v1; the DHT key is its SHA-256 hash. Every Concord node in the world computes byte-identical keys with zero coordination. This is what content-addressed means: the name is derived from the content, not assigned by an authority. The value is not the data. Concord stores no data in the DHT. It stores a provider record: a small note saying "peer P can serve key K, and here are P's current ad

h: 4.5 What "advertising under a rendezvous key" means
t: Put the two halves together and the mechanism is almost anticlimactic. Every Concord node, on startup: computes the key from concord/dht/v1, calls Provide on it, republishing every 3 hours, and calls FindProviders on the same key every 15 seconds, dialling anything new that comes back. The DHT is not being used as storage. It is being used as a mailing list: the key means "I am a Concord node", and the value is where to find whoever said so. That is a rendezvous point, an agreed-upon location where parties who have never met can each leave a note for the other. Two consequences: The key is gue

Concord does not have "a discovery mechanism". It has four, tried in this order, and only two of them involve a server of any kind: Rung 1, mDNS. Multicast DNS is DNS shouted at a local network instead of asked of a server: a UDP packet to a multicast group that every machine on the segment receives. Concord broadcasts under its own service tag so it only finds other Concord instances, and dials anything that answers. Multicast is blocked on plenty of corporate and locked-down networks, and Android's sandbox denies the socket that the implementation needs, so its failure is logged and ignored

There is a fifth path, and it is the one most people use first. An invite code is a compact base64 blob you paste into a chat, carrying the guild's opaque handle and name, the inviter's peer ID, the inviter's current addresses, and the rendezvous list the inviter is using. It is discovery by human courier: the joiner's app configures itself entirely from the code, dials the addresses it names, and asks to join. Two details in the implementation. h: 5. Reachability: NAT, hole punching, and relays
t: Alice now has an address for Bob. That does not mean she can reach him.

h: 5.1 What NAT is, and why it breaks inbound connections
t: Your home router owns a single public IP address. Your devices have private addresses (192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x) that mean nothing on the internet. The router performs Network Address Translation: on the way out it rewrites the packet's source address and port to its own, and records the substitution in a table so that replies can be rewritten back. The critical detail is that the table entry is created by an outbound packet. An inbound packet that matches no entry names no internal destination the router could compute, so it is discarded. This is why you can browse the web from behind a NAT and

If a NAT entry is created by an outbound packet, then two NAT'd peers can create entries for each other by both sending at once. That is hole punching. Two things must be arranged, and neither peer can do them alone: each must learn its own externally observed address (which requires someone outside to tell it), and the two sends must be simultaneous within roughly a round-trip time. libp2p's answer is DCUtR, Direct Connection Upgrade through Relay. The two peers first establish a relayed connection (§5.3), then use that channel to exchange their observed addresses and to measure the round-tri

h: 5.3 Circuit relay, and why it cannot read what it carries
t: When punching fails, packets have to go through somebody. libp2p's Circuit Relay v2 provides that, and its structure is the reason a relay is not a server. Mechanically: Alice holds a reservation with the relay, so it will accept circuits addressed to her. Bob asks the relay to connect him to Alice; the relay splices his stream to hers and forwards bytes. Alice and Bob then run their own Noise handshake end-to-end over that spliced pipe, and that is the whole argument: The relay is not an endpoint of the A↔B session. It forwards the outer ciphertext of a handshake it is not party to. It cannot

h: 5.4 Why a relay is a fallback and not the norm
t: Latency. Two hops through a third machine instead of one, plus whatever detour its geography imposes. Throughput. Bounded by the relay's link and by explicit resource limits, but not by a per-circuit meter. On the rendezvous: 512 reservations, 64 concurrent circuits, 8 reservations per peer and 16 per IP. On a peer relaying for friends: 32 reservations, 8 circuits, 4 per peer and 4 per IP, because it is somebody's laptop rather than a server. There is no per-circuit byte or duration cap, and that absence is load-bearing rather than generous: a relay advertising any limit makes every connection

h: 6.6 The GIF proxy, the one place the node does work on your behalf
t: Everything else the rendezvous carries is ciphertext. GIF search is different in kind, and the reasoning is the interesting part. A GIF picker that calls the provider's API directly from the client sends every keystroke of every search, and every member's IP address, to that provider. The usual fix is for the platform to proxy the search itself, which does not remove the leak — it relocates it, to the company running the platform, who then see the searches instead of the provider. Concord relocates it too, to the rendezvous you already run and already connect to constantly: the same trade, mad

A server is something whose correct behaviour you depend on. This is not that. The distinction is testable: assume the node is fully malicious and enumerate the damage. It can refuse service, return nothing, drop bytes, count bytes, correlate IP addresses and timing, and read a guest's leg of a meeting. It cannot read a member's message, forge one, join a group, learn a roster, or keep your history. And the system is built so that its absence is a degradation rather than an outage (§6.5). That is what "untrusted" means here: not "we promise not to look", but "looking would not help".

h: 7. Group encryption: MLS, epochs, and membership with no arbiter
7.1 Why pairwise encryption is not enough
t: Encrypting a two-person conversation is a solved problem. A group is not, and the two reasons are separate: Cost. Sealing each message separately for every recipient is O(n) work and O(n) bandwidth per message, and establishing sessions after a membership change is O(n²). Agreement. Far more importantly, pairwise sessions have no shared notion of "the group". Two members can hold different beliefs about who is in it, forever, with no mechanism that notices. In a system with no server to be authoritative, that is fatal: encryption is the only thing deciding who can read, so "who is a member" mu

h: 7.2 The ratchet tree, an epoch, and a commit
t: MLS arranges members as the leaves of a binary tree. Every node in the tree holds a key pair. A member knows the private keys along its own path to the root and no others. The root secret is the group secret. That structure is what makes group rekeying cheap: O(log n) ciphertext for a full group rekey, rather than O(n). Two terms follow directly: An epoch is a version number for the group. Each epoch has its own key schedule derived from that epoch's root secret. Epoch e's secrets are derived from epoch e−1's plus fresh entropy, forward only, through a one-way key-derivation function. A commit

h: 7.3 Forward secrecy and post-compromise security, concretely
t: These two phrases are used loosely everywhere. Here is what they mean here, including their limits. Forward secrecy: compromise now does not retroactively open the past. When the group advances from epoch e to e+1, epoch e's secrets are deleted, and they cannot be recomputed from e+1's because derivation runs one way. An attacker who takes your device today, with today's keys, cannot open traffic sealed in previous epochs. The limit, stated plainly: forward secrecy protects captured network traffic. It does not protect your local database, which holds your decrypted history sealed under a key

h: 7.4 Authorising membership changes with no server to arbitrate
t: Two questions that look like one, and separating them is the whole design. Who is a member? Answered cryptographically, not administratively. You are a member if and only if you hold a leaf in the ratchet tree. There is nothing to consult and nothing to disagree about. Who may change membership? Answered by a signed, replayable governance log that every peer folds into identical state. The trust anchor is the current owner, and current is doing real work. The founding key, the account stamped into the guild when it was created, is only the seed the replay starts from. Ownership then moves alon

h: 7.5 What this design costs: no merge
t: There is no conflict resolution for concurrent commits, and pretending otherwise would be the hand-waving this document is trying to avoid. Two authorized members who commit at the same epoch fork the group. One branch loses. Its members do not reconcile; they recover by being re-welcomed. A heal loop notices the group is stranded, finds an authorized committer that is online, sends a fresh key package, and joins at the current epoch, overwriting its local group state. Local mitigations keep this rare (a mutex serializes add-and-publish on one node; the first commit seen at an epoch wins the l

The cipher suite is MLS suite 0x0001 (MLS_128_DHKEMX25519_AES128GCM_SHA256_Ed25519), chosen because its signature algorithm is Ed25519, the same algorithm as a Concord account. That alignment buys a real property: the MLS signing key is derived from your seed by HKDF-SHA256 with the label concord-mls-sig-v1, so a restarted device recomputes it and keeps signing with nothing to back up. (On a linked device the MLS credential is the device certificate and the signing key is the device key itself, so the same property holds per device.) h: 9.1 Media is peer-to-peer and never touches the backend
t: Text is small and delay-tolerant. Audio and video are large and real-time, and the browser already has a well-tested stack for that. So Concord splits the job: the browser does the media, Go does the matchmaking. There is no media code in the Go tree at all: no WebRTC stack, no track handling, no mixer, no forwarding unit. h: 9.2 IP privacy: the state of it
t: WebRTC connects peers directly. That is the point, and it has a consequence: each participant learns the others' IP addresses. Among friends this is unremarkable, and equally true of BitTorrent and most VoIP. For a meeting link you paste somewhere public it is a deanonymization vector: a stranger who clicks it sees your home IP, and you see theirs. The standard fix is a TURN relay. When a client sets its ICE transport policy to relay-only it offers only relayed candidates, so its real address never leaves the machine. If both ends relay, media flows client → relay → client and neither particip

Sometimes the person you want in a call should not have to install anything: a client, a contractor, somebody who will be in one meeting. Guests are that path, and they are the one place Concord relaxes its trust model, so the relaxation is bounded on every axis.

The gateway is a dumb pipe: it dials the host (reachable because the host holds a relay reservation with that very node), forwards newline-delimited frames in both directions, and keeps no state. It does not validate the token, because it cannot: it has never seen one. It does not read the meeting. The token is a 24-byte bearer secret from a cryptographic random source, not a signed structure. There is nothing to verify because there is nothing to verify against: the host looks it up in its own table. That table is persisted in the host's encrypted database, so a link mailed out on Monday stil

h: 10.2 What a guest can and cannot reach
t: Can: send and read chat in one channel of one meeting; see the last 30 messages of it; join the call with audio; turn on camera; share their screen. They appear in the roster explicitly labelled as a guest, under a self-asserted display name that is sanitized of characters that could fake formatting or a mention. Cannot: reach any other channel (there is no frame that changes channel); reach any other guild; read history beyond those 30 messages; hold an identity, a key package, or a leaf in the MLS group; be verified; appear in a member's contact list; or persist beyond the meeting. The guest's own leg is readable by the gateway. A guest has no identity, so there is no key to encrypt to and no handshake to bind: their traffic is TLS to the gateway and then Noise to the host, never plaintext on the wire, but the gateway is an endpoint of the first hop. Member-to-member traffic in that same meeting stays end-to-end encrypted and unreadable to it; the guest's own messages, in that hop, are not. That is the price of "no install". It is not fixable without giving guests identities, at which point they are members, and it is why guests are meeting-scoped, single-channel, capped

h: 11.2 Catching up with nobody holding anything for you
t: With no server buffering messages, a peer that was offline has to ask. The protocol is a direct peer-to-peer request: Details that matter: The cursor is per channel, taken as the latest of sent and updated, so a reaction or a pin on an old message brings it along too. It is backdated by five minutes to absorb clock skew between two machines that trust no clock. The responder answers only members, checked against the connection's authenticated identity. Membership is not a courtesy here: add commits carry joiners' key packages in the clear, so serving them to a non-member would leak the roster.

Images and files never travel inline. Each is sealed with a fresh random key, content-addressed by the SHA-256 of its ciphertext, and referenced from the message body by a token carrying the blob identifier and the key. Nothing it did not already hold. Tokens are keyed by the opaque 16-byte mailbox tag, never by identity, so the token store says "this device wants waking for this mailbox" and cannot be turned into a member list. The wake itself carries no content — the node has never had plaintext to put in it. Wakes are collapsed to at most one per mailbox per 30 seconds, and a token not refreshed in 60 days is forgotten (clients re-register on every login).

h: Intended follow-on: "Stay connected" once push works
t: Android's "Stay connected" preference runs a foreground service so the process survives backgrounding. It exists precisely because there is no push: without it, a closed app receives nothing until reopened. It also costs a permanent notification in the tray and keeps a libp2p node running on the user's battery. Once push is configured, that trade changes — a wake can start the process on demand — and the preference should default off for builds where pushAvailable() is true, while staying on where it is false.
